# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What made the others more pressing?

whys.g1: Lena and Aisha both put safety and insurance ahead of yield and sit together under a plain name, while my answer about pulling cash back fast to pay bills and Rachel's about runway and the accountant's tax reason are different reasons that rightly stay out of that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all four answer why the other things mattered more than yield.

founder.order_why: The window question (4) sits between two screens that ask the same context question (3 and 5), so the context step reads as interrupted rather than built up in sequence; the rest flows logically from context to problem to sending.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the identical prompt 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks who decides and pays: at a startup the founder-CEO signs off on where the reserve sits and the board may have to approve the cash policy, separately from the finance lead who moves the cash. Nothing captures the cost I care most about, yield given up on a long-term reserve, as opposed to fees and hours. The flow also never asks whether cash sits in plain checking rather than the bank's treasury product; screens 8 and 9 assume the treasury product.

PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 3 nearly overlap: once I've said yes, the cash sat there the whole time, so 'how many of the last 3 months' just repeats it (3 of 3).
PRIMARY.missing: Whether I ever compared the default treasury yield against moving cash elsewhere (T-bills, an outside money market fund) and what made me decide the switching and operational burden wasn't worth a higher yield; also nothing on safety, like FDIC/sweep coverage or concentration risk after SVB, or how much of the raise sits there versus in operating accounts.

screens.why7: Count, order, own-first and the rivals' shape are met, but the own row restates the circumstance instead of the hurt, which the card forbids, and that makes the belief read nearly circular.
screens.instead: Own row 'Earning more on the reserve without added risk', then the same four rivals: Knowing the months of runway left · Keeping cash safe above the insured limit · Getting cash back fast when needed · Moving money between accounts without mistakes

screens.why1: After the pain and its rivals, asking how we handle the reserve today and how well that goes is the obvious next step before any talk of Palus.
screens.why2: "Until the company sends it today" stopped me: it should say *spends*, and the trailing "today" reads as if the sending happens today, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: Where the long-term reserve sits and what it nets after fees is the thing a finance lead looks at every month on the treasury dashboard.
screens.why4: The two boxes take the act and the rungs I typed, and *I'm not sure* is the right escape for a founder who can't say.
screens.why5: My job was "until the company spends it"; the screen's "sends it" changes the meaning a little, though my typed answer is kept word for word.
screens.why7: My four rungs sit on one measure (rate after fees), best to worst, with a working first rung ("Earned a market rate after fees"), but my second box never says where good enough ends, so the line falls to the default.
screens.instead: Today, where do finance leads keep raise cash they won't touch for months, and what does it earn after fees? (Say which results are good enough.)

screens.why1: Right after I said how finance leads handle raise cash today, it makes sense to check the five ways that can turn out before strangers see them.
screens.why2: 'Market rate' and 'after fees' are everyday words to a startup finance lead comparing a bank's treasury against T-bills or a money market fund.
screens.why3: A finance lead sees the yield and fees on the treasury statement every month, so they can say roughly where their last quarter landed against market.
screens.why4: The first four rungs are a clean ladder on one measure, but the last one switches from an outcome to a method (cash in checking) and overlaps with 'next to nothing after fees', so someone who kept cash in checking could pick either.
screens.why5: These are my own after-fees rungs as I saved them, and nothing about Palus, bonds or my fee leaks into them.
screens.why7: The measure is yield after fees, there are five rungs best to worst, rung 1 works, the line under rung 2 leaves both sides answerable, and the escape is apart; but rung 5 names a different place for the cash than the act being tested ('the bank's treasury product'), so the worst rung is not the same act failing.
screens.instead: Earned a market rate after fees · Earned a bit under market after fees · ┄ line ┄ · Earned well under market after fees · Earned next to nothing after fees · Earned nothing at all on the reserve

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out to finance leads, after the context and problem screens are settled.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a play button and a plain note on cost and delivery; I can answer on first read, though the hint is long.
screens.why3: Picking the voice my study goes out in is my own decision as the founder, made by tapping and listening.
screens.why4: Two distinct, playable voices with a sensible default; no escape is needed because the hint says people can read and type instead.
screens.why5: It still says finance leads and asks only about the interviewer, so nothing of my product or roles leaks to the respondent.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks, deciding how a finance lead answers is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are plain to a startup founder; the name Daphne is explained in its own line.
screens.why3: I know how finance leads at funded startups work (in Slack and email, between tasks), so I can pick the format they would actually finish.
screens.why4: The three options cover voice, text and both, with no overlap, and each says what the respondent does.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and 'finance leads' is my own actor as I typed it.

screens.why1: After choosing how finance leads answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending, and as a founder whose batchmates asked for this I know exactly whom I'd send it to.
screens.why2: Plain words a founder uses every day: people I know, a list I found, one link posted where they gather; only 'the Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's layout, which by screen 16 I would.
screens.why3: It asks about my own outreach, which I know cold: I would send it to batchmates and founders in my network by name.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people are distinct and cover the real cases (my network, a sourced list, a YC Bookface or Slack-style group post), and a choice screen like this needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is restated or bent here; it is a neutral send step and my pick, people I know by name, stands as I made it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right under the title, with the number that decides it beside it (Frequency, median 1.5 months out of 3 against my 2 to 3), and the line under it says the stage takes its worst card.
screens.why_b2: The tally (2 holding, 2 split, 7 answered) and each card's bar read plainly, but '6 TO 7 COUNTED' in the kicker and Frequency's three ways of saying the same split (3 vs 3, 3 of 6 below, 1 short) took me a second look.
screens.why_b3: The statement is my launch post nearly word for word (18 to 24 months of runway, about 3.5%, 0.15% to 0.60% fee), and the four beliefs are the ones I checked, in my terms.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what a half-split on how often finance leads face this decision means for Palus. For example, it doesn't say whether the reserve decision is a one-off after a raise rather than a monthly one, so I'm left to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: 'Among these 7' is a fair hedge, but nowhere does it say seven people is a small sample, and Current solution is called 'Holding up' when it lands exactly on the bar at 4 of 6.
screens.instead: Seven finance leads answered, so read this as a first signal: all 7 keep raise cash in the bank's treasury and 4 of 6 say it falls short, but only half face the decision month after month and only half rank it in their top two. Next, test whether this is a one-time decision after a raise rather than a monthly one.

screens.why_b1: The verdict (holding up, above my band) sits right beside the number that decides it, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells all for me, a marker at 5 labelled as my bar (at least 6 in 10), and an axis of 0 to 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the belief, but it says only 'finance leads', dropping 'at startups holding cash from a raise', and it counts the setup every one of my customers is in (cash in the bank's treasury product) rather than the cost I care about, the yield given up; 'the most recent time it happened' tacked onto a yes/no question also reads oddly.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' with a pointer to the next two cards is a signpost, not a meaning; it never says that a 7-of-7 yes on where the cash sits tells me little about whether founders feel the lost yield.
screens.why_b5: 'A small group: a lean, not a call' keeps n honest, but 'holding up above your band' on 7 of 7 still reads as a confirmation when the question asked about the routine almost every Mercury or Brex startup follows, so a No was hardly possible.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 keep raise cash in their bank's treasury product: a lean from a small group, and nearly everyone in this segment does this, so it says little about whether the yield they give up hurts; the next cards test that.

screens.why_b1: The status word "People disagree" sits right beside the deciding number (3 of 6 at or beyond my 2 to 3 months, bar 4 of 6, 1 short), and the median of 1.5 agrees with it.
screens.why_b2: Months out of 3 per person, 6 counted, and the marker at 4 of 6 are all plain at first look; the axis starting at 0 is only a small oddity, since nobody could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Frequency and the belief is my clause and my range (keep raise cash in the bank's default treasury product, 2 to 3 months out of 3), with my actor shortened to "Finance leads" but plainly mine.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" only points onward; it never says what a 3-3 split on how often my people sit in the bank's treasury means for Palus, such as whether the monthly cash review is really my occasion.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ("a lean, not a call") and Lena's guess is set apart, but the Asked line's trailing "the most recent time it happened" contradicts a months-count question and blurs what people actually answered.
screens.instead: Drop "the most recent time it happened" from the Asked line, and make the So line say: a split, so for half of them the bank's treasury isn't a standing monthly habit; test whether the monthly cash review is the right moment before building around it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *People disagree* sits right beside 3 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6, 1 short, so I know it did not hold and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 6 people, two picks each, 12 picks in all, my row is marked as the problem I named, and the strip's marker at 4 shows the bar against 3 for, so I see what is counted, over whom, and where the bar sits on first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the belief, but *Choosing where the raise cash sits* is my circumstance said back to me rather than my pain, which was earning more on the reserve without switching banks or risking it, and *Finance leads* drops the 'at startups holding cash from a raise' I typed.
screens.why_b4: The So line usefully notes my problem ties with knowing the months of runway left, but stops at 'the 3 who ranked others first are below' without telling me what that means for the idea, such as selling the yield as extra runway against the safety and liquidity worries in the quotes.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Lena's guess named), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and a 3-3 split is called disagreement, not support.
screens.instead: 3 of 6 put choosing where the raise cash sits in their two, 1 short, tied with runway; the 3 against wanted safety, insurance and fast access, so pitch the yield as extra months of runway and lead with how safe and quick to withdraw the reserve is, then ask more founders.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '4 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6 · at the bar', so I know the belief held and that it held exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: Each rung shows its count and whether it counts for or against, the line is drawn under 'Earned a bit under market after fees', and the strip shows 4 of 6 with the marker at 4, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits read at a glance.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' and 'keeping the money in the bank's treasury product still falls short' are my claim in my words: the problem is the treasury product bundled with the bank, not the bank.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic hand-off; it does not say that one more person above the line would flip this, or that the gap sits with people earning well under market or nothing.
screens.why_b5: It says the group is small ('a lean, not a call') and keeps n visible, but it counts Tomás, whose cash sat in checking and never in a treasury product, as the treasury product falling short; without him the result is 3 of 5, under the bar.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 4 of 6 at a bar of 4, a lean from 6 people, and one of the four (Tomás) had no treasury product at all; ask more finance leads who actually use Mercury or Brex Treasury before leaning on this gap.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *People disagree* sits right beside *3 of 6 put it in their two · bar 4 of 6 · 1 short*, so I can see the line missed by one person.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief about choosing where the raise cash sits among five hard things are the line I checked, in the words I typed.
screens.why_b4: The quotes suggest I should lead with safety and same-week access rather than yield, but the screen never says what the miss means for Palus; *When a line fails* is just a heading.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 3 against, yet the groups add to 4, and the *safe and insured (2)* group shows only Aisha, so Lena, who is marked not counted, seems to be inside a counted group.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that a finance lead's risk is being asked why money was lost, not why it earned less, or that the board watches insurance after the bank failures, or that an accountant wants plain cash for the tax break; these add to my belief that yield is the pull.
screens.instead: Group counts that add to the 3 counted against, with Lena shown apart, plus one line: safety above the insured limit and fast access beat yield for these finance leads, so pitch Palus as safe and liquid first and the higher yield second.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I'm in the segment, a startup banking with Mercury, Brex or similar, which is exactly what a gate should do before anything else.
screens.why2: Mercury and Brex are plain to me, but 'a similar startup bank' is fuzzy: I'd pause over whether SVB-at-First-Citizens or a big bank's startup program counts, and over whether a secondary account at Mercury counts when most cash sits elsewhere.
screens.why3: I run our accounts, so I know where we bank without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate; a startup with Mercury plus a sweep or treasury account elsewhere is still a clean Yes.
screens.why5: It names only the banks the segment is defined by and says nothing about any product, yield idea or plan.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes; or No' is easy to hold, though §17 would have it simply as 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its cash at Mercury, Brex or a similar startup bank? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury, asking about where our raise money sat in the last quarter is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say 'cash from the raise', not 'raise cash', and 'the bank's default treasury product' makes me stop: do they mean Mercury Treasury, the sweep, or just the checking account it lands in?
screens.why3: I know exactly where our cash sat over the last 3 months, it's my job.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chip 'I can't recall one particular cash balance' makes no sense to me here, because nobody thinks of their cash as 'a balance' they had one time.
screens.why5: 'Default treasury product' sounds like someone's pitch talking, as if they're setting up the case that leaving money in the bank's option is the mistake, and it isn't wording I'd use.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to answer by ear.
screens.why7: Some people would honestly say No, like the ones who moved cash to a brokerage or T-bills, but the question asks where the cash sat, not what went wrong, so I'd say Yes happily: I chose that on purpose and 3.2% is fine by me.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you leave cash from your raise earning less than you could have got somewhere else? Yes or no.

screens.why1: It follows the gate in order, but once I've said yes I keep the raise in Treasury, the count is already answered: it sits there every month, so it feels like the gate asked twice.
screens.why2: I'd say 'our Mercury Treasury' or 'the money market sweep', not 'raise cash' or 'the bank's default treasury product', so I'd read it twice to be sure it means the same thing.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our cash sat each month; I'd answer 3 without guessing.
screens.why4: 1, 2, 3 and I can't recall are complete and distinct, but for a balance that never moves only 3 is ever a real answer, so the other buttons are dead.
screens.why5: 'Default treasury product' and 'raise cash' read like someone else's framing of my setup, not how a finance lead talks, so the founder's angle shows through a little.
screens.why6: It's one short question with the unit said once and 'a number from 1 to 3, or say you can't recall'; I'd hear it once and answer.
screens.why7: The units, the 1-to-3 buttons and the escape are all right, but the event is a standing state (cash kept in a fund), the card's named pitfall, so anyone past the gate says 3 and the count can't speak to how often the problem hits.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 3 months did you move cash between checking and your bank's Treasury account? 1 · 2 · 3 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking whether and how often I kept raise cash in the bank's treasury product, asking which part of handling that cash I'd most like easier follows naturally.
screens.why2: 'Your last months after a raise' made me stop: is it the last 3 months, or the stretch after our last raise? The options themselves are words I use every day.
screens.why3: These are all things I handle myself as the person running our accounts and cash, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: 'Keeping cash safe above the insured limit' and 'Getting cash back fast when needed' are really the things I weigh when choosing where the raise cash sits, so they overlap with that row instead of standing apart.
screens.why5: Choosing where the raise cash sits is the founder's problem in my words, and nothing about a product or their terms reached me.
screens.why6: One short question and five parallel phrases with one escape said last, easy to hold by ear, though the anchor sounds a little clumsy.
screens.why7: The own row is present and not first, there are four rivals and None of these is at the first ask, but two rivals are parts or causes of the own row, which bends the no-overlap rule.
screens.instead: Think of the last 3 months. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Knowing the months of runway left · Moving money between accounts without mistakes · Choosing where the raise cash sits · Reconciling balances across our accounts · Getting payments approved on time · None of these

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, asking why those mattered more is the natural follow-up.
screens.why2: It reads back my picks as long paraphrased rows, and choosing where cash sits is not how I would put it, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly why liquidity and moving money matter to me, since the operational burden is what I care about.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options shown.
screens.why5: Choosing where cash sits sounds like the founder's framing of the decision rather than my words, a slight drift but no product leak.
screens.why6: One question and short enough, but hearing two picks set against a third in one breath is a mouthful to hold.
screens.instead: You said getting cash out fast and moving it between accounts mattered most. Why those, more than where the cash is held?

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I kept raise cash in the bank's treasury product, asking how that went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Treasury product', 'market rate' and 'after fees' are my words, but 'your last cash balance' isn't an occasion I can picture, so I'd read the stem twice to work out what time it means.
screens.why3: I know roughly what we earned (about 3.2%), but whether that was 'a bit under' or 'well under' market is a guess, and for me the job was mostly about safety and not having to babysit it, which none of this asks about.
screens.why4: The rungs are parallel and there's a working one, but 'a bit under' and 'well under' market have no edge I could place myself against, and the last rung (cash in checking) describes not using the treasury product at all, not how using it went.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but the job 'keep the money safe and earning' has narrowed to earning alone, which drifts from what was meant and from the access and moving-money worries I picked one screen ago.
screens.why6: Heard once it works: a short stem, five short parallel options I can hold, and one escape said last, though 'after fees' four times is a little heavy.
screens.why7: The shape holds (five rungs best to worst, a working first rung, a fail-outright last rung, one escape apart, so the belief can be both supported and refuted), but the measure bends: it is yield alone rather than the job's safe-and-earning, and the last rung switches act from the treasury product to checking.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you checked where your raise cash sat. How did keeping it in the bank's treasury product go? Earned about what we expected, no hassle · Earned a little less than expected · Needed manual sweeps or moves to keep it earning · Couldn't get cash out when we needed it · Ended up sitting in checking earning nothing · Someone else did it

screens.why1: It follows straight from my answer on the last screen, so it's obvious why they're asking what makes the bank's treasury setup work for us.
screens.why2: It plays back my answer as "keeping the money" instead of "keeping cash in the bank's treasury product", and "What keeps it working?" leaves a bare *it* I have to work out.
screens.why3: I know exactly why it works: it's the bank's default, there's nothing to set up or reconcile, and the operational burden matters more to me than a bit more yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product leaks, but "keeping the money" has drifted from the treasury product the earlier screens asked about.
screens.why6: Two short sentences and one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said keeping raise cash in the bank's treasury product works for you. What makes it work?
